title: Why did London burn in 1666?
subtitle: Four days of flames
subject: histoire
description: On September 2, 1666, a bakery fire escaped from Pudding Lane. Four days later, 13,000 houses and St Paul's Cathedral were in ashes, with only six recorded deaths.
author: benjamin-campbell

hero.hook: A baker's oven, a strong wind and a city of wood: that was all it took to wipe out medieval London.

blocks.text: On **September 2, 1666**, a fire broke out in a bakery on [[Pudding Lane]] in London. What began as a small blaze became one of the most destructive fires in the city's history. The flames burned for **four days**, destroying around **13,000 houses** and much of the medieval city, including [[St Paul's Cathedral]].

Several witnesses of the time recorded the scale of the destruction, among them [[Samuel Pepys]], a senior naval administrator and member of the British Parliament. In his diary, he described the fire spreading across London, the mounting destruction and the confusion of those trying to escape. But how did a fire that began in a bakery grow large enough to destroy most of the city?

sections.title: A city of wood driven by the wind

blocks.text: In **1666**, most of London's buildings were made of timber. Many houses had thatched or pitch-coated roofs, materials that caught fire easily. Buildings were packed together along narrow streets: in places, houses on opposite sides almost touched. The fire found ideal ground on which to spread.

blocks.caption: Remains of the fires of 1666 and 1940 at St Bride's, London: charred wood, bell fragments, glass distorted by heat.

blocks.text: The wind made everything worse. A strong gust blew just as the fire began to spread, pushing the flames westward toward the rest of the city. Burning pieces of wood and thatch flew through the air and started new fires ahead of the main blaze. The fire was nothing exceptional in itself: it was the crowded streets and wooden structures that gave it everything it needed to run.

In 1666, London had no official fire department. Volunteers took to the streets with water pumps, leather buckets, hooks and axes, hoping to stop the fire from spreading further. They tried to demolish buildings ahead of the flames to open a [[firebreak]], a gap the fire could not cross.

But there was hesitation at first about pulling down homes and businesses, which probably helped the fire spread. [[Thomas Bloodworth]], the Lord Mayor of London, did not immediately order large-scale demolition. By the time major firebreaks were organized, it was already too late.

Some historians argue that Bloodworth's hesitation is what let the fire spread so far. But London's response was also limited by the tools and level of organization available at the time. The city simply faced a disaster it was not prepared to handle.

The fire destroyed most of London, yet the death toll appears remarkably low. Records of the time count only around **six deaths**. Set against the thousands of buildings that went up in smoke in four days, the figure seems almost impossible.

blocks.caption: Londoners fleeing by boat on the Thames as St Paul's burns: a painting by Philippe-Jacques de Loutherbourg, c. 1797.

blocks.text: In reality, nobody knows how many people really died, and some historians think there were more. London's poorest residents left few written records: deaths caused indirectly by the fire were never recorded. Another explanation: the fire spread fairly slowly at first, which gave residents time to escape. The physical destruction was immense, but the number of recorded deaths stayed low.
The blaze was so hot that it melted pottery and glass. Archaeologists have found materials melted or fused together by the heat, proof of just how intense the fire was.

After the fire, London changed face. The authorities adopted new building regulations that restricted timber and pushed builders toward stone and brick. Many streets were widened, so that a future fire would find it harder to jump from one front to the next.

blocks.caption: The relief on the Monument to the Great Fire (1677), near Pudding Lane: Charles II comes to the aid of the City.

blocks.text: The disaster also got people thinking about insurance. Before 1666, few of the city's residents had any kind of protection against such losses. Afterward, new schemes began to emerge and paved the way for the modern [[fire insurance]] that many people still use today.

The fire of London revealed a pattern that still shapes our cities. A major disaster exposes a city's weaknesses, in how it is built and how it is protected, and forces people to rethink the safety of those who will live there next.
London burned because a cramped city of wood with no fire brigade met a strong wind and a response that came too late; from its ashes came brick building codes and fire insurance.

sources.text: S. Pepys, The Diary of Samuel Pepys, éd. R. Latham et W. Matthews, vol. 7, University of California Press, 1972.
J. F. Field, London, Londoners and the Great Fire of 1666: Disaster and Recovery, Routledge, 2018, p. 20.
